performers: Peter Pears, tenor; Dennis Brain, horn; Boyd Neel String Orchestra; Benjamin Britten, conductor
intro: Peter Pears and Dennis Brain, the soloists Britten wrote the Serenade for, recorded it for Decca in 1944 with the composer conducting the Boyd Neel String Orchestra. The Dirge, its fifth movement, fills one 78 side.

sections.label: Var 8 · Last stanza, tenor ends alone
sections.mNote: The first stanza’s words return; the tenor ends alone.

cues.title: Tenor alone, first stanza
cues.text: The Dirge opens with the tenor unaccompanied. His part carries a single marking, come un lamento, and singers have followed Pears in keeping to a steady mezza voce. The anonymous fifteenth-century text has nine stanzas, each ending “And Christe receive thy saule”.
cues.evidence: Herbert Glass, programme note for the Los Angeles Philharmonic: the Dirge’s vocal line has “no dynamic or expressive marking other than the initial come un lamento” and is usually sung, following Pears’s example, in a constant mezza voce: https://www.laphil.com/works/serenade-for-tenor-horn-and-strings . Colin Clarke, Seen and Heard International, 11 April 2024, on the unaccompanied opening of the Dirge: https://seenandheard-international.com/2024/04/britten-sinfonias-typically-adventurous-programme-mixing-a-world-premiere-with-music-of-today/ . Nine stanzas of the text: Wikipedia, Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serenade_for_Tenor,_Horn_and_Strings ; Boosey & Hawkes calls it the anonymous 15th-century Lyke Wake Dirge: https://www.boosey.com/cr/music/Benjamin-Britten-Serenade/3880

cues.title: Strings enter beneath the voice
cues.text: The strings join from the second stanza, under the same six-bar tune in the tenor. Christopher Palmer wrote of “a fugally impelled funeral procession” in the orchestra, with a voice “impassively independent” of it.
cues.evidence: Palmer’s description, quoted in Herbert Glass’s programme note for the Los Angeles Philharmonic: https://www.laphil.com/works/serenade-for-tenor-horn-and-strings . Richard Cooke, conductor, blog 16, 13 July 2020, describes the movement as built round a constantly repeated six-bar theme in the tenor, with the tenor alone at the start: https://www.richardcooke.org/blogtext.htm?blog=64 . The Gramophone, December 1945, on the Dirge: the double-basses “begin a fugue which increases in tone”: https://archive.org/details/sim_gramophone_1945-12_23_271

cues.title: First performance, Wigmore Hall, 1943
cues.text: Pears and Brain gave the first performance of the Serenade at the Wigmore Hall on 15 October 1943, with a string orchestra conducted by Walter Goehr. This Decca recording was made in 1944, with Britten conducting the Boyd Neel String Orchestra.
cues.evidence: Premiere: Herbert Glass, Los Angeles Philharmonic programme note, https://www.laphil.com/works/serenade-for-tenor-horn-and-strings ; Wigmore Hall as venue: Wikipedia, Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serenade_for_Tenor,_Horn_and_Strings . Recording: Philip Stuart, Complete Decca Classical Discography 1929–2009, session 0288 (Pears, Brain, Boyd Neel String Orchestra, Benjamin Britten; 25 May and 8 October 1944), https://archive.org/details/DeccaComplete

cues.title: Britten on Dennis Brain
cues.text: Britten met Brain in 1942, when Brain was first horn in the RAF Orchestra and Britten was writing radio scores for it. After Brain’s death in 1957 Britten wrote that “His help was invaluable in writing the work”.
cues.evidence: Britten’s memorial tribute to Brain (1921–57), quoted in Herbert Glass’s Los Angeles Philharmonic note, https://www.laphil.com/works/serenade-for-tenor-horn-and-strings , and in Jon Kochavi’s Sun Valley Music Festival note, which gives Britten’s account of the RAF Orchestra and the radio commentaries of 1942: https://www.svmusicfestival.org/program_notes/program-notes-stories-and-poems/

cues.title: Horn enters at “From Brig o’ Dread”
cues.text: The horn enters in the sixth stanza, at “From Brig o’ Dread when thou may’st pass”, with the music the cellos and basses had at their own first entry. Palmer wrote that the procession comes “close enough to strike mortal terror”, with “horn hysteria”, and then “makes off”.
cues.evidence: Richard Cooke, conductor, blog 16, 13 July 2020: the volume rises until the horn’s dramatic entry at “From Brig o’ Dread”, which has the same music as the cellos and basses at their first entry: https://www.richardcooke.org/blogtext.htm?blog=64 . Christopher Palmer’s description, quoted in Herbert Glass’s Los Angeles Philharmonic note: https://www.laphil.com/works/serenade-for-tenor-horn-and-strings . Colin Clarke, Seen and Heard International, 11 April 2024, notes that Britten builds slowly to the horn’s entry in the Dirge: https://seenandheard-international.com/2024/04/britten-sinfonias-typically-adventurous-programme-mixing-a-world-premiere-with-music-of-today/

cues.title: Ninth stanza, repeat of the first
cues.text: The ninth stanza repeats the first: “This ae nighte, this ae nighte, / Every nighte and alle”. The tenor ends alone, as he began. Palmer wrote that the procession leaves the last word to “the disembodied wail and whine of the singer”.
cues.evidence: Text of the nine stanzas: Wikipedia, Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serenade_for_Tenor,_Horn_and_Strings . The tenor begins and ends alone: Richard Cooke, blog 16, 13 July 2020, https://www.richardcooke.org/blogtext.htm?blog=64 . Palmer’s words, quoted in Herbert Glass’s Los Angeles Philharmonic note: https://www.laphil.com/works/serenade-for-tenor-horn-and-strings

transitions.title: Horn takes up the cellos’ music
transitions.how: The tenor repeats one six-bar tune through every stanza. Over stanzas two to five the strings accompany it and the volume rises. At “From Brig o’ Dread” the horn enters with the music the cellos and basses played at their first entry. After this stanza the music subsides.
transitions.evidence: Richard Cooke, conductor, blog 16, 13 July 2020: a constantly repeated six-bar theme in the tenor; the volume rises to the horn’s entry at “From Brig o’ Dread”, which repeats the cellos’ and basses’ first-entry music, after which the movement subsides: https://www.richardcooke.org/blogtext.htm?blog=64

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Peter Pears (tenor), Dennis Brain (horn), Boyd Neel String Orchestra (string orchestra), Benjamin Britten (conductor)
fields.note: The Internet Archive creator field lists Pears, Brain and the Boyd Neel String Orchestra. The CHARM record names Britten as conductor, and Philip Stuart’s Decca discography lists Pears, Brain, the Boyd Neel String Orchestra and Britten for the session. The first performance, in 1943, was conducted by Walter Goehr (Herbert Glass, Los Angeles Philharmonic programme note).

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: The Dirge alone, on one side of the six-side Decca set AK 1151–53: side 4 of 6, matrix AR 8464. The other sides carry the Prologue and Pastoral (sides 1 and 2, the second also with the Nocturne), the Elegy (side 3), the Hymn and the start of the Sonnet (side 5) and the end of the Sonnet with the Epilogue (side 6).
fields.note: The titles of the six sides in the CHARM record and the Internet Archive items show the Dirge on a side of its own. That the side holds the whole movement is inferred from the side’s length (4 min 14 s) and from the neighbouring sides, which begin and end with other movements; no source states the movement’s duration or compares the side with the score.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Stuart’s discography records the Serenade sessions as 25 May 1944 and says three sides (8461, 8464 and 8466) were re-made on 8 October 1944. The side transferred here is AR 8464, take 4, one of the three re-made sides, so its date is inferred to be 8 October 1944; the discography does not say which take was issued, and the whole Serenade was recorded in May and October 1944.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The discography lists the 25 May 1944 session at West Hampstead Studios, Decca’s London studios, and gives no separate venue for the October re-make.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The Internet Archive item gives the label as Decca and the speed as 78; Stuart’s discography lists the Serenade among Decca’s UK 78 rpm issues. The record size is not stated in the sources consulted.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: Decca AK 1153 (third disc of the automatic-coupling set AK 1151–53), issued in the UK in November 1945
fields.note: The file name of the transfer is AK_1153_AR_8464-4. Stuart lists the issue as “(Nov45) (A)K1151-53”, and says UK release dates come from Decca’s monthly supplements or from advertisements and reviews in The Gramophone. The December 1945 issue of The Gramophone reviews the set as “Decca K1151-3 … Auto AK1151-3”. The same six sides were also issued in manual sequence as K1151–53, in which the Elegy and the Dirge share K1152 (Decca advertisement, The Gramophone, February 1946); the disc transferred here is the automatic coupling AK 1153, which carries the same two sides.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: AR 8464, take 4 (side 4 of 6); AR 8463 take 2, the Elegy, is on the other side of the same disc
fields.note: From the item metadata and the CHARM record, which list the six sides of the set as AR 8461-4, AR 8466-4, AR 8462-3, AR 8465-4, AR 8463-2 and AR 8464-4.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The item names no transfer engineer. It belongs to the Internet Archive’s Centre for the History and Analysis of Recorded Music (CHARM) 78rpm collection and carries a CHARM record (METS_AK_1151, created 30 January 2009 by conversion from a spreadsheet).

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Internet Archive lists the item as added on 15 January 2019; that is the upload, not the date of the transfer.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: The item states no stylus, equalisation or noise reduction. The MP3 is the Internet Archive derivative of the uploaded FLAC.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: In copyright. Britten died on 4 December 1976, so the Serenade is protected in the EU and the United Kingdom (life plus 70 years) until the end of 2046; Boosey & Hawkes is the publisher. The poem is anonymous and fifteenth-century.
fields.note: The publisher is documented by the Boosey & Hawkes page. The term is a calculation from the composer’s death date, which the composer chapter on this site gives. Rights in the composition are separate from rights in the recording and do not block publication.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU and UK public domain: first published before 1963 (Decca AK 1151–53, November 1945). United States status not established.
fields.note: The release date is Philip Stuart’s, taken from Decca’s monthly supplements or from The Gramophone; The Gramophone for December 1945 independently reviews the set as already on sale. For a recording first published in 1945 the Copyright Office describes a term of 95 years plus 5 years after first publication in the United States, to the end of 2045; whether that term applies to this British issue was not established. The item carries no licence statement and sits in the CHARM collection, not in the Great 78 Project; its metadata carries no litigation, takedown or restriction flag.

composer.epithet: Composer who wrote Grimes and Aschenbach for Peter Pears, a work with an ark full of animals for Suffolk children, and a requiem in which dead soldiers speak.
facts: Frank Bridge privately; Royal College of Music, 1930–33, with John Ireland
Lowestoft and London; North America, 1939–42; then Suffolk

composer.background:
Benjamin Britten grew up in a house facing the North Sea at Lowestoft. His father was a dentist; his mother, Edith, sang and encouraged his music. Born on St Cecilia’s Day, 22 November 1913, he learnt piano and viola and filled exercise books with compositions. At the Norwich Festival in 1924 he heard Frank Bridge conduct The Sea. In 1927 his viola teacher, Audrey Alston, introduced him to its composer.

Bridge took him on. The lessons could be uncomfortable. “I used to get sent to the other side of the room,” Britten recalled in the Sunday Telegraph in 1963; “Bridge would play what I’d written and demand if it was what I’d really meant.” In 1937 he thanked his teacher with the Variations on a Theme of Frank Bridge, ten variations for strings, among them a waltz, a funeral march and a fugue.
